Same game records, a different target: an ordinal class from a bag of games
Official Task 2 topic page [9]; training rank labels come from the same 1,000,000-game collection.

Task 2 of the competition. Each question is a bag of 5, 10, 15 or 20 games by one player; we output one of ten ordered rank classes. Exact class scores 1, adjacent class e^-1. Because the classes are ordered, both the loss and the decision rule should use that order. Same 1,000,000 training games; 800 test questions.
Two model families produce log-probabilities over the ten classes
Blend weights 1 (bag LMs) and 2 (HumanSL sequences) were fixed on 800 held-out players; no tuning on the private split.
Six bag-level fine-tuned language models and fourteen HumanSL sequence Transformers. Log-probabilities are averaged inside each family, blended 1 to 2, and decoded with the expected-score rule.
Soft labels over neighbouring classes; decide by expected score
a class between the plausible ones
Diaz and Marathe, Soft Labels for Ordinal Regression, CVPR 2019.

SORD gives each class a soft target that decays with distance from the true class, so the model is penalised less for near misses. The decision then maximises expected competition score, which favours a central class when the posterior is spread over neighbours.
The frozen human-move network, read as a per-move strength signal
KataGo b18c384nbt-humanv0 [5] is an external, frozen network; run in PyTorch with KataGo sources.

For every move of a game we ask the frozen KataGo HumanSL network how likely that move was under eight rank profiles, plus entropy, top-1 agreement, win rate and score lead. A small Transformer reads the 250-ply feature sequence, is pooled over the bag and trained with SORD. Fourteen seeds and data subsets are averaged.
HumanSL sequence features gave the largest single gain
Source: results/task2_scores.csv; task2/REPRODUCE_TASK2_BEST.md. Website scores are public interim results.

Website score by stage: language model alone 0.3976, SORD 0.6236, HumanSL gradient boosting 0.6915 and 0.7006, bag models plus HumanSL sequences on 100 plies 0.7248, 250 plies 0.7676, three extra 350-ply models 0.7683. The jump from 0.7248 to 0.7676 is the main finding.
Late-game moves carry rank information; beyond 250 plies the gain is within noise
* rank_hsl7 used 100-ply features with fewer models; website blends differ in other components, so the gain is not attributed to plies alone.
Source: results/task2_scores.csv; task2/REPRODUCE_TASK2_BEST.md. Website scores are public interim results.

Re-extracting HumanSL features for plies 101-250 improved a matched held-out gradient-boosted model from 0.6859 to 0.7083 and the website blend from 0.7248 to 0.7676. Plies 251-350 showed no clear gain in a matched test (0.6989 vs 0.7039 validation) and a 0.0007 website gain, so we treat them as ensemble diversity, not a finding.
Bag term helps, extra fine-tuned LM hurts, seeds saturate
Source: results/task2_scores.csv; task2/REPRODUCE_TASK2_BEST.md. Website scores are public interim results. Axis truncated.

Eight variants uploaded on November 21-22. Removing the bag models costs 0.0157, adding a fine-tuned game-level LM costs 0.0212, and seven, eleven and fourteen sequence models differ by under 0.002, so seeds are saturating.
Interim result: 0.7683, rank 15 of 165 on 22 November
Submitted file e13 SHA-256 09c1a5a5dce8eef3...bb59d0d (results/task2_best_prediction.csv); recipe in task2/REPRODUCE_TASK2_BEST.md.

Best file e13 scored 0.7683, rank 15 of 165 on 22 November. Local held-out differences below 0.005 did not predict the website order, so we report only public scores. Reproduction: artifacts for CPU byte-identical regeneration, scripts and seeds are in the repository; GPU retraining gives a close but not identical file. The external HumanSL network and official data are required.
